newsitem.title: UK: European firms totally unprepared for EMU - survey.
newsitem.headline: European firms totally unprepared for EMU - survey.

text.p: Most top European companies have made no attempt to estimate the cost to their business of the single currency, slated to start in less than 24 months, a survey by British management consultant firm KPMG showed.
Of 301 major European firms asked, 80 percent said they could not estimate the cost to their business of the changeover to the euro. Only eight percent quoted a figure.
But a hefty majority of the companies -- 93 percent of those surveyed -- said they expected the country in which they were based to join Economic and Monetary Union at some stage.
"Many companies are seriously unprepared for the big changes EMU will bring," Alan Reid, European head of KPMG Management Consulting, told a conference to present the survey on Thursday.

"Given that over half of all respondents believed their country will enter EMU at the earliest possible date, the 80 percent of companies that have failed to undertake such a fundamental estimate have very little time in which to prepare."

KPMG conducted the poll in July and August of 1996 by telephone, talking to finance directors of firms across all sectors employing at least 5,000 people and with a European headquarters in one of the member states of the European Union.
Britain, Ireland, France, Germany, Italy, Austria, Greece, Spain, Portugal, the Benelux countries and Scandinavia were included.
Not one firm, asked to state the key issues it faced in the area of international business on trade, mentioned Europe's planned single currency, the survey showed.

But prompted into addressing the prospect of EMU, 45 percent said they would put EMU towards the top of a list of important issues facing their firms, while 22 percent said they would put it towards the bottom.

While almost three-quarters of top European companies said they expected to benefit from a single currency, two thirds of those asked said they had no strategy for coping with the introduction of the euro, although half of those said they were in the process of developing one.
German-based firms had the greatest number of strategies already in place, at 52 percent, while only 19 percent of British-based companies and 25 percent of Italian-based had a working plan.

"We found the Italians were the most enthusiastic about setting things in motion," said KPMG's chief economist Vicky Pryce, noting that 69 percent of firms based in Italy said they were developing plans to cope with the advent of the euro.

On the cost side, while very few companies were prepared to estimate the extent to which the changeover would tip their balance sheets, of the eight percent that did, the projections ranged from one to 65 million sterling ($1.6 to $106 million), with 20 percent estimating costs of over 20 million sterling.

Change to information technology (IT) was picked out as the area expected to induce most cost, but only four percent of the 301 firms said they had completed a review of IT systems in prepartion for EMU.
In the whole of Britain, Spain, Portugal, Greece and Austria, not one firm had conducted and completed a review, although 67 percent said they were currently undertaking one.
More than a third of companies surveyed across Europe had not yet started looking at IT preparations for the euro. ($1=.6161 Sterling)
